questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a price-triggered service belong in an off-chain backend rather than relying on Chainlink Automation here?
options: Chainlink Automation is deprecated (per Lesson 19's live finding), so the honest, fully-in-your-control alternative is an off-chain Node service doing the same job
Chainlink Automation never supported threshold-based triggers of any kind
Smart contracts cannot read price feeds under any circumstances
Off-chain services are always faster than on-chain automation, regardless of deprecation status
questions.explain: The lesson ties this directly back to Lesson 19's finding that Automation is deprecated, making an off-chain polling service the honest alternative covered here.

questions.q: Why does this lesson's code call `feed.decimals()` instead of hardcoding 8 when scaling the price?
options: Not every feed uses the same number of decimals, and hardcoding it would silently break if the code is later pointed at a different feed
decimals() is required by Solidity syntax and cannot be omitted
Hardcoding 8 would cause the contract call to revert with an error
decimals() returns the feed's contract address, not a scaling factor
questions.explain: The lesson explains this explicitly — most USD feeds use 8 decimals but not all do, so calling decimals() avoids a silent, hard-to-catch bug.

questions.q: What problem does tracking `wasAbove` and checking for a crossing solve in the polling loop?
options: It stops the service from re-triggering on every single poll while the price simply stays above the threshold, firing only when the state actually flips
It prevents the service from ever reading the price feed more than once
It encrypts the price value before it's used in a transaction
It automatically adjusts the threshold value based on market volatility
questions.explain: The lesson explains the crossing check specifically prevents repeated firing every tick the price happens to stay above threshold — it only acts the moment the boolean state changes.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what pattern from earlier chapters does `triggerAction`'s transaction-sending code reuse?
options: Chapter 1's send-a-transaction pattern, including the nonce and gas-estimation handling from Lesson 5
Chapter 3's subgraph mapping handler pattern
Chapter 2's chain-reorg handling logic
Lesson 21's Sign-In with Ethereum message format
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls back to Chapter 1's transaction-sending pattern and Lesson 5's nonce/gas handling as what triggerAction reuses.

questions.q: What honest tradeoff does this lesson identify for a self-run price-triggered service compared to a managed oracle network?
options: No decentralization, no redundancy, and no on-chain guarantee it's even running — in exchange for full control and low cost
It's strictly worse in every respect, with no offsetting benefit mentioned
It has every guarantee a managed oracle network has, with no tradeoff at all
It only works on testnets and cannot submit real mainnet transactions
questions.explain: The lesson states this tradeoff directly: the service gains simplicity, full control, and low cost, while giving up decentralization, redundancy, and any on-chain guarantee of uptime.
